newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra - GST push unhelpful.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Inside Canberra - GST push unhelpful.

text.p: (From the "Inside Canberra" newsletter)

Government strategists are concerned the demands for a goods and services tax (GST) by business bodies such as the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and by Liberal self promoters such as Jeff Kennett, could well kill any chance of a tax being introduced in the next parliament.

The strategy of the government has been to stick to the pre-election promise not to introduce a GST in the current parliament and avoid giving any commitments, one way or another, for the next parliament.
This is becoming increasingly difficult as the business crescendo for a GST rises.
Kim Beazley declared firmly this week Labor would continue to oppose a GST.
Before long Kim Beazley will be demanding from Howard a "rock solid" promise not to introduce a GST in the next parliament.
Howard will attempt to avoid doing this, but if business continues to make noisy public demands for a GST, Howard will be pursued by the media to give a firm "yes" or "no" statement.
And the more he stalls, the more he will be pursued.
It will be a replay of the lead up to the 1993 election and the struggle over "Fightback!"
CAMPAIGN FORGOTTEN
Business boosters for the GST appear to have forgotten how difficult it was to sell a GST (so difficult that Keating won an election on it) and Howard on Wednesday reminded them.

He played down the GST as an "economic elixir" for Australia adding: "There is also the danger in the present atmosphere that people who are advocating things like the GST forget that there is still a lot of entrenched opposition to it in the community."
This point was emphasised only this week by Toby O'Connor, National Director of the Australian Catholic Social Welfare Commission.
He emphasised the New Zealand experience showed compensation packages to lower income groups to offset the cost of the GST are easily devalued.
Indside Canberra makes the point that from the moment John Hewson launched the GST plenty of groups were in favor of it; just as long as the tax didn't apply to them.
There is of course no reason why an imaginative treasurer could not rejig the existing wholesale sales tax (WST) system to do much of what the GST did.

The WST need not apply to business inputs a la the GST and the cost of this concession could be funded by a tax on accomodation beds, airline tickets, insurance premiums, taxi fares and many other service charges now outside the scope of the WST.
And the beauty of such an approach is Howard would not have to telegraph it before the election, but could do it after he had safely won a second term.
JEFF NOT HELPFUL TO HOWARD
There is deep suspicion in the Howard camp as to Jeff Kennett's motives in coming out last week urging a GST.
Everyone in politics knows what Kennett's real attitude is towards Howard -- he hasn't the guts to be a good prime minister.

Kennett has appeared to lean over backwards in his public statements since the federal election supporting Howard, but some of his utterances, such as those on the GST, have not been helpful to Howard.
There is a strong body of opinion among Victorian Liberals that Kennett, 49 on March 2, has ambitions for a shot at federal Liberal leadership.
It goes without saying he would regard himself as far more qualified than the main contenders, Peter Costello (whom Kennett refers to as "Dog") and Peter Reith.
But then there is no sign Howard, having struggled all these years for the prime ministership, is going to give up the job after two terms.
One ex-Howard staffer says that the prime minister "will be harder to get out than Hawkie -- they'll have to blast him out."
-- Inside Canberra 61-6 273-1600
